title: Epidemiology and Prevention of HIV (Including PrEP)

questions.stem: A 27-year-old bisexual man presented with a request for postexposure HIV prophylaxis after sexual intercourse. He had not used barrier protection. He asked for advice about routes of transmission of HIV .
questions.lead_in: What poses the highest risk of HIV transmission?
questions.explanation: Receptive anal intercourse. Receptive anal intercourse carries a significantly higher risk of HIV transmission than any other sexual activity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q34

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man attended for routine follow up. He was asymptomatic. He was known to have HIV and was taking a fixed-dose regimen of abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine He was last screened for STI 6 months previously. He was sexually active, and reported three casual male partners in the previous 3 months. He reported that he discloses his HIV status to partners. He engaged in anal receptive and oral insertive and receptive sex. He used condoms for anal sex most of the time. On examination, his oropharynx was clear. His urogenital examination was without discharge, lymphadenopathy, or unusual skin findings. Rectal examination was performed, and no abnormalities were noted. Investigations: CD4 count 900 cells/mm3 HIV viral load undetectable
questions.lead_in: What screening tests should be performed?

options.text: No screening is recommended at today’s visit. Screen annually
Urine and rectal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, oropharyngeal screening by culture for N. gonorrhoeae plus syphilis serology
Urine, rectal, and oropharyngeal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis
Urine, rectal, and oropharyngeal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis plus syphilis serology
Urine screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis

questions.explanation: Urine and rectal screening by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, oropharyngeal screening by culture for N. gonorrhoeae plus syphilis serology This patient has high risk for exposure to STI. In this case, STI screening is recommended at 3- or 6-month intervals. Screen urethral (urine) and rectal sites by NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis . Oropharyngeal screening for C. trachomatis is not recommended. NAAT or culture can be used for oropharyngeal screening for N. gonorrhoeae. Note that some NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae are less sensitive because they cross react with other Neisseria spp. found in the oral environment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q23

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman attended clinic to discuss her birthing plans. She was 37+5 weeks gestation in her first pregnancy. She had HIV and was taking tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine and boosted atazanavir and reported full compliance. Investigations: CD4 count 456 cells/μL HIV RNA <40 copies/mL
questions.lead_in: What delivery plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Elective cesarean section at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine commenced at least 3 hours prior
Elective cesarean section at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine commenced at least 3 hours prior plus single dose nevirapine
Elective cesarean section at 38 weeks without intravenous zidovudine
Spontaneous vaginal delivery provided obstetrically permitted with intravenous zidovudine during labor
Spontaneous vaginal delivery provided obstetrically permitted without intravenous zidovudine during labor

questions.explanation: Spontaneous vaginal delivery provided obstetrically permitted without intravenous zidovudine during labor Intravenous zidovudine should be administered to women with HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL (or unknown HIV RNA) near delivery but is not required for women receiving ART regimens who have HIV RNA ≤1000 copies/mL during late pregnancy and near delivery and no concerns regarding adherence to the ART regimen. Scheduled cesarean delivery at 38 weeks’ gestation (compared to 39 weeks for most indications) is recommended for women who have HIV RNA >1000 copies/mL near delivery. https://aidsinfo.nih.gov/co ntentfiles/lvguidelines/PerinatalGL.pdf
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q22

questions.question: An HIV positive male is currently not an ARV. His CD4 is 865 and VL 2000. He would like to resume sexual intercourse but wanted information about how to be as safe as possible.

parts.text: Counsel this patient on methods for safer intercourse (3 things).

cohort_answer.text: Consistent condom use or delay sexual intercourse until fully suppressed (80% effective); PEP 80%; Initiate ARVs immediately 40-99% effective; Pre-exposure ppx for partner (99% for non ivdu, 70% for ivdu); Screen and treat other STIs.

questions.question: Lady otherwise healthy with recent febrile/mononucleosis syndrome and now HIV + with prior negative 6 mth ago

parts.text: Would you recommend treatment?
Her seroconversion has now resolved when she sees you. She has a seronegative partner and they wish to stay together "forever." Give 2 clinical outcomes that treatment have been shown to improve?
Give 3 options for transmission prevention to sero-negative male partner with the relative % risk reduction of each in isolation.

cohort_answer.text:
Would you treat: Yes.
Clinical outcomes: Reduces AIDS related and non-AIDS related morbidity and mortality; Decreases transmission; Improves CD4 recovery.
Transmission prevention options: Viral suppression of infected partner 99% (treatment as prevention) – HPTN 052 + PARTNERS study; PrEP for uninfected partner (95-99%); Condoms 90-95% (when used appropriately)

questions.question:
Q12 (2018)
28M sustains needlestick injury. It was a used needle from his uncle who is an injection drug user and shares needles with others.

parts.text: A) What is the risk of transmission, assuming he is non-immune and does not receive any interventions, if the uncle is seropositive for the following: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV
b) According to the recommendations, name TWO preferred regimens to minimize transmission of HIV and ONE alternative regimen which can be used:

cohort_answer.text: Risk: Hepatitis B ~30% (HBsAg+/HBeAg-: 25%; HBsAg+/HBeAg+: 27-62%); Hepatitis C ~3% (1.8%, range 0-7%); HIV 0.3% (hollow bore needlestick 0.23%). Preferred PEP regimens: TDF 300mg + FTC 200mg daily + Raltegravir 400mg BID x28 days; TDF 300mg + FTC 200mg daily + Dolutegravir 50mg daily x28 days (repeat serology at 0,3,6 months). Alternative: TDF 300mg + FTC 200mg daily + Darunavir/Ritonavir daily x28 days

questions.question: Kid punctured himself with diabetic uncle who is HIV pos and not on ARV, pokes himself twice daily. Kid is taken to emerg, finger still bleeding.

parts.text: 4 risk factors for HIV transmission
What is the risk of transmission?
What would you put the kid for PEP
How long would their PEP be for?

questions.model_answer:
a) Four risk factors for increased HIV transmission risk after a percutaneous exposure: (1) deep puncture/injury. (2) Visible blood on the injuring device. (3) A device that had been placed in the source patient's artery or vein (e.g., large-bore hollow-bore needle). (4) High viral load in the source patient (e.g., advanced HIV disease/AIDS, or not on suppressive antiretroviral therapy).
b) Risk of transmission: the average risk of HIV seroconversion after a percutaneous needlestick exposure to HIV-infected blood is approximately 0.3%.
c) PEP regimen: a 3-drug regimen, e.g., tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor such as raltegravir or dolutegravir.
d) Duration of PEP: 28 days.

questions.question: MSM

parts.text: 4 specific indications for PrEP
You are seeing every 3 mos, name 5 specific tests you should order

questions.model_answer:
a) Indications for HIV PrEP: (1) Condomless anal or vaginal sex with a partner of unknown or HIV-positive status (especially if that partner is not virally suppressed). (2) A bacterial STI (syphilis, gonorrhea, or chlamydia) diagnosed in the past 6 months. (3) Repeated or recurrent use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). (4) Injection drug use with shared needles/equipment, or a sexual partner who injects drugs.
b) Tests to obtain every 3 months on PrEP: (1) HIV antigen/antibody test (to confirm continued HIV-negative status before continuing PrEP). (2) Serum creatinine/eGFR (renal function monitoring, given tenofovir's nephrotoxic potential). (3) Syphilis serology (RPR/VDRL). (4) Gonorrhea and chlamydia NAAT testing at all exposed sites (urethral, rectal, pharyngeal). (5) Pregnancy test, where clinically applicable.

questions.question: Refugee woman, HIV +ve, VL 72,000

parts.text: When should you start her on ART and what 3 regimens are approved to give in pregnancy
What do you suggest for her intrapartum antiretroviral treatment and what mode of delivery.
Now you have a 6 hour old neonate, mom's VL is now 2,700. What ART regimen do you start and for what planned duration.
What test should you do on the neonate and what is the ideal timing of the test.
In Canada what kind of feeding is recommended and why?

questions.model_answer: a) Start ART as soon as possible regardless of CD4/gestational age to achieve suppression by delivery. Approved in pregnancy: (1) Dolutegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine (or lamivudine). (2) Raltegravir + tenofovir/emtricitabine. (3) Ritonavir-boosted atazanavir or darunavir + tenofovir/emtricitabine. b) Intrapartum: continue oral ART; if VL >1000 copies/mL near delivery add IV zidovudine infusion during labour and recommend scheduled cesarean section at 38 weeks; if VL <1000, vaginal delivery is acceptable and IV AZT not required. c) Neonate (mom VL 2700, i.e. >50-1000): infant should receive combination ART prophylaxis (zidovudine + lamivudine + raltegravir/nevirapine) rather than AZT monotherapy for 4-6 weeks given detectable maternal VL. d) Neonatal HIV DNA/RNA PCR testing: at birth (or by 14-21 days), again at 1-2 months, and again at 4-6 months. e) In Canada, formula (replacement) feeding is recommended regardless of maternal VL/ART, to eliminate residual risk of postnatal HIV transmission via breastmilk.

questions.question: PrEP with TDF/FTC in the MSM population.

parts.text: Give 4 indications for HIV PrEP in this population
Give TWO regimens (as you would describe them to a patient) for PrEP in MSM

questions.model_answer:
a) Indications for HIV PrEP: (1) Condomless anal or vaginal sex with a partner of unknown or HIV-positive status (especially if that partner is not virally suppressed). (2) A bacterial STI (syphilis, gonorrhea, or chlamydia) diagnosed in the past 6 months. (3) Repeated or recurrent use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP). (4) Injection drug use with shared needles/equipment, or a sexual partner who injects drugs.
b) Two ways to describe dosing to the patient: (1) Daily continuous dosing - one tablet of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (300 mg/200 mg) taken every day, without interruption. (2) Event-driven "2-1-1" on-demand dosing (for MSM with anticipated intercourse) - 2 tablets taken 2-24 hours before sex, then 1 tablet 24 hours after the first dose, then 1 more tablet 24 hours after that (a total of 4 tablets around each sexual encounter).

parts.text: 2 ways to prevent transmission and % efficacy

cohort_answer.text: Prevention: Suppress his viral load (>99% efficacy); PrEP for wife while VL not suppressed (99%). Factors affecting transmission: Viral load; Compliance with treatment; At risk behaviour (active STI lesions). Transmission for 1 unprotected encounter: 0.1%.

parts.text: 2 ways to prevent transmission and % efficacy

cohort_answer.text: Treatment as prevention – virtually no sexual transmissions occurred once virally suppressed (HPTN 052, PARTNER 1+2, Opposites Attract); anyone starting ART should use another form of protection for the first 6 months until VL<200; PrEP >90% efficacious

cohort_answer.text: Viral load; Adherence; Genital ulcers/STI; Circumcision (if Female +, Man -). Also: Type of sex (anal receptive > insertive anal > receptive vaginal > insertive vaginal >> oral); presence of active STI leads to 2-5x increased risk; barrier protection used

questions.question: Needlestick injury from HIV+ patient

parts.text: A. Name four factors that influence risk of transmission and state whether they increase or decrease risk.

cohort_answer.text: Source patient: On treatment - decreased risk; VL suppressed - decreased risk (U=U). Body fluid: true vascular puncture - increased risk; Visible blood on needle - increased risk; Unused needle - decreased risk. Degree of exposure: superficial stick no puncture wound - decreased risk; Hollow bore needles higher risk than solid instruments. CDC case-control study: Deep injury (OR 15); Device visibly contaminated with blood (OR 6.2); Needle placement in vein or artery (OR 4.3); Terminal illness in source patient/AIDS (OR 5.6). Majority injured by hollow bore vs solid needle

questions.question: Needlestick

parts.text: A) HIV PEP

cohort_answer.text: Start antiretrovirals as soon as possible, ideally within 1-4 hours of injury. Prophylaxis not indicated if cannot be initiated within 72 hours. Duration of prophylaxis 28 days. Risk of acquiring HIV from hollow-bore needle with blood from known HIV-seropositive source 0.2-0.5%. PEP options: RAL + TDF/FTC; DTG + TDF/FTC. Risk of transmission ~0.3% (mucosal exposure ~0.03%). Clean wound with soap and water, confirm true exposure, obtain baseline serology (HBV, HCV, HIV), repeat HIV serology at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months

questions.question: PrEP.

parts.text: 4 reasons in MSM to go on prep
Labs to order every 3 months (5)

cohort_answer.text: Canadian PrEP guidelines (https://www.cmaj.ca/content/cmaj/suppl/2017/11/21/189.47.E1448.DC1/170494-guide-1-at.pdf): Emtricitabine, TDF. Reasons: Condomless anal sex within last 6 months with any of: infectious syphilis or rectal bacterial STI (particularly if diagnosed in preceding 12 months); recurrent use of non-occupational PEP (more than once); ongoing sexual relationship with HIV positive partner with non-suppressed viral load; high-incidence risk index (HIRI-MSM) risk score >=11. Labs q3 months: HIV, syphilis, C and G testing (depending on sites of sexual activity), Creatinine, pregnancy testing if indicated

questions.question: A patient with MSM who has insertive anal intercourse presents to the clinic:

parts.text: What are 4 indications for PrEP.
b. 2 dosing regimens for DTG/FTC as you would prescribe in clinic.

cohort_answer.text: a) Any person with a sexual partner with HIV and detectable VL; MSM and transgender women who (last 6 months) engaged in condomless anal sex and/or had documented STI; non-occupational PEP use >1 in past year; heterosexual men with condomless sex with female partners in HIV epidemic region; people who inject drugs and share needles; heterosexual men diagnosed with STI or condomless sex with high-risk partners (sex workers, IVDU). b) TDF/Emtricitabine (can be event driven, 2-1-1 dosing: 2 pills 2-24h before sex, 1 pill 24h after first dose, 1 pill 24h after second dose); TAF/Emtricitabine (daily therapy); Cabotegravir LA (monthly x2, then q2 months).

parts.text: 4 indications in MSM to go on prep
Labs to order every 3 months

cohort_answer.text: HIV PrEP Indications: Cis-men and transgender women with condomless anal sex within last 6 months and any of: a) Infectious syphilis or rectal bacterial STI, particularly if diagnosed in preceding 12 months; b) Recurrent use of non-occupational PEP (more than once); c) Ongoing sexual relationship with HIV positive partner with non-suppressed viral load; d) High-incidence risk index (HIRI-MSM) risk score ≥11. Also PWID within 6 months who report needle sharing. Labs q3 months (CDC): HIV 4th gen Ab/Ag + VL; STIs: syphilis, GC+C; Cr q6 months if age>50, Cr q12 months if age<50. Canada GLs: HIV test, Cr, syphilis, GC+C, pregnancy
